Actual Article Body:
In rival Victorian election campaign launches, Labor pledges $1.17bn for elective surgeries while Liberals say they will send young offenders to boot camp

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

As Ben Carroll arrived at a Melbourne community centre to launch Labor’s Victorian election campaign, he had to squeeze his way through a crush of party faithful, clad in red and already a little sweaty.

The Kellaway community centre in Moonee Ponds in the city’s inner north-west was so packed on Sunday that some supporters were left waiting outside.

It was a far smaller venue than the theatre in Cranbourne where Daniel Andrews launched Labor’s 2022 campaign. It was also in the seat of Essendon – a traditionally safe Labor stronghold the party has held at all but one election since 1979 but which it fears it could lose at this month’s election, despite a 12.5% margin.

With polls showing Labor’s primary vote slumping into the low 20s, and one survey published last week putting it at just 18%, Carroll had the task of lifting the spirits of a party facing the prospect of a historic defeat.

He put public healthcare at the centre of the launch, leaning heavily on the party’s credentials as the “party of Medicare” and its commitment to a “first-class public health system”. He announced a $1.17bn commitment to perform an additional 100,000 elective surgeries in public hospitals and halve the waiting list, alongside more than $195m for 500,000 additional specialist appointments.

The announcement contrasts with the Coalition’s plan to spend $1.27bn paying private hospitals to perform procedures for public patients, which the opposition has said will come at no cost to patients.

“Labor believes in public healthcare, the Liberals don’t,” Carroll told the crowd of about 250 people. “As for One Nation, they don’t even believe we should have a health department.”

He accused the opposition of laying the groundwork for an “American-style health system”, warning: “It won’t cost you until it does.”

Carroll’s wife, Fiona Rothville, gave the crowd a personal account of the public hospital system’s role in saving their daughter Madeline’s life after she stopped growing in utero at 20 weeks and was born at 37 weeks weighing just 1.8kg.

“As for me, I developed pre-eclampsia and spent two and a half weeks in hospital on a different ward on a different floor,” she said. “These doctors and nurses saved the life of our daughter, and they saved my life...
